description: Sterling's design rules and patterns. Sections are the rules components and screens follow; patterns are complete compositions with numbered steps. Components point here from components.json (related).

sections.name: Principles
sections.summary: A good component is easy to use correctly and hard to use incorrectly. This table lays out both positive and negative design principles.

rows: Used for differences in structure, state, type, and size
Including choices that properties could handle multiplies variants beyond what's maintainable
Expose what product designers need to change
Too few — product designers detach it
Too many — combinations the author never intended
Fixed sizing; text overflows instead of wrapping
Overly complex nesting and poor naming
Object-oriented abstractions (grid composed of child components)
A single component for a complex pattern (grid)
States, by control type — hover, focus, disabled, selected (interactive controls); error (inputs, status); loading, empty (data views)
Missing states (e.g., no hover on a button)
Edge cases — long text, negative numbers, large values, empty data
Accessibility — visible focus, contrast in every mode, signals beyond color (icon, sign, or label)
Color as the only signal (e.g., gain/loss in green/red only)
Designed with engineering, so it can be built
Props shared with code — one definition
Breaking changes after release — removing properties or restructuring layers resets overrides on component instances
Use when / don't use when guidance
Lack of guidance leads to misuse (e.g., switch vs. checkbox)
No owner, so teams build their own variations

sections.name: Accessibility
sections.summary: Visible focus, contrast in every mode, and signals beyond color.

rules.text: Every interactive control has a focus variant (State = focus, or a combined -focus value) with a 2px focus/ring outline. It sits outside the control (3px) by default; inside for grid cells, header cells, and tabs, which touch their neighbours; and 1px inside the warning or error border on flagged cells, so both stay visible. The outline is its own layer, so focus never shifts the layout.

Text needs 4.5:1, and large text and UI graphics (icons, borders, focus rings) need 3:1 — in Light and Dark. Every pair a component uses is listed in tokens.json contrast.rules, and npm run contrast must pass. Disabled content is exempt (WCAG 1.4.3).

Pair every color signal with an icon, sign, or label: status chips have a tone icon; gain and loss cells show ▲ / ▼ and a + / − sign; side chips say Buy or Sell; errors and warnings add an icon and helper text; selected rows also check their checkbox; selected tabs add an underline and a bold label.

Every field has a visible label. Hide it (Show label off) only when a visible label sits right next to the field, and give the field an accessible name in code. Icon buttons always set Label: it's the accessible name and the tooltip.
Skeleton bars are decorative. Pair them with "Loading…" text, and mark the region aria-busy in code.

doDont.title: Gain and loss: glyph and sign, not just green and red
doDont.do: Gain / loss cells add ▲ / ▼ and the sign, so the direction reads without color.
doDont.dont: Color alone: unreadable for color-blind users, in grayscale, and on some displays.

doDont.title: Fields: always a visible label
doDont.do: The label stays visible while the field has a value, and names the field for assistive tech.
doDont.dont: No label: once a value is entered, nothing says what the field is.

sections.name: Data display
sections.summary: Numbers are the content: never hide digits, and line them up.

rules.text: Text (labels, names, text cell values) truncates with an ellipsis at a max width. Numbers never truncate — hidden digits are a risk in financial data.

Width = characters × 7.5 + 24, rounded up to 8 (numericColumnWidth() in the plugin); add 16 for the gain / loss glyph, or for the warning / error icon in a column whose cells can be flagged. Size for the longest value the column can hold.
Numeric columns use the Numeric style (tabular figures) and right alignment, so digits line up. Numeric headers are right-aligned too.
Size numeric and identifier columns (IDs, codes, reference numbers) to their values. When a grid has room to spare, only descriptive text columns (names, notes, reasons) stretch to take it up.

Only the sorted column shows a sort icon: ↑ ascending, ↓ descending. An unsorted, sortable header shows no icon at rest and reveals ⇕ on hover and on keyboard focus, so a grid shows at most one sort icon at rest. Sortability stays discoverable through that hover and focus icon and a pointer cursor; in code, set aria-sort on the sorted header. Turn Show sort off for a column that can't be sorted.
The sort icon always sits next to its label: immediately after a left-aligned label, immediately before a right-aligned one. A right-aligned label stays flush with the values below it.

The Figma header cell approximates that rule: its label fills the cell, so the icon sits at the cell's edge. For numeric columns, size the column to its values (numericColumnWidth()) and the icon lands beside the label; in a left-aligned column the icon stays at the right edge. The coded header keeps the icon beside the label at any width.

Sterling's grids are for reading, sorting, selecting, and acting in bulk, so in code a grid is a table: Tab moves between the header sort buttons and the row checkboxes, and screen readers use their table commands. Cell-by-cell arrow keys (an interactive grid) are for editable cells or cells with several controls. Focus variants are for future editable cells; read-only grids show focus on header buttons and row checkboxes only.
Chips keep a fixed size; density changes the row around them. That holds for status and side chips. A filter chip is a control, so it follows the small control height like a small button.
Summary metrics show a compact value (e.g. $12.35B) with the full value in Detail.
Tabs separate scopes; views are named filter sets; every applied filter is a chip; criteria that define a dataset are not filters.

doDont.title: Numeric columns: right aligned, tabular figures
doDont.do: Right-aligned tabular figures: units, tens, and decimals line up, so values compare at a glance.
doDont.dont: Left-aligned: magnitudes don't line up, so 84.50 looks as big as 1,250.00.

doDont.title: Truncate text, never numbers
doDont.do: Text may truncate: the full value is in a tooltip or detail view.
doDont.dont: A truncated number hides digits — size the column for the longest value instead.

sections.name: Naming
sections.summary: Names match code, and stay stable once released.

rules.text: Every component sits under a slash folder (Controls, Chip, Grid, Icon, Input, Overlay, Summary, Tabs) with a self-describing last segment, because the Assets panel shows leaf names. Turn on Show subfolders in the Assets panel to browse by folder.

Sentence case in Figma, one-to-one with camelCase code props (Show icon ↔ showIcon). Kind = visual style · Tone = semantic color · Size = dimensions · State = the element's UI state · Status = a condition of the data · Checked = checkbox value · Show … = every boolean.
Keep layer names stable (Label, Value, Icon, Glyph). Overrides follow layer names, so renaming a layer resets instance overrides for it.

Figma has no property aliases, so rename in place: the plugin renames existing variants (legacyVariantName) and properties (previousNames), keeping every instance linked with its variant and overrides.

sections.name: States
sections.summary: Every state a control needs, in one State property, with no invalid combinations.

rules.text: Interactive controls: default, hover, pressed, focus, disabled, and selected where it applies. Inputs and cells: error and warning. Data views: loading and empty.
State holds the element's UI state — interaction, plus selection and validation where the element has them. Conditions of the data use Status (e.g. Summary metric over-target).
Where two states happen together, add a combined value instead of a second axis: selected-hover (rows, cells), error-focus and warning-focus (inputs, cells), selected-focus (tabs).
A warning or error cell keeps its tinted fill, border, and icon while its row is hovered or selected. A flag is never hidden by another state.
Every combination of variant properties exists and looks right (e.g. Summary metric has all four Status × State variants; loading looks the same for both Statuses).

sections.name: Color
sections.summary: Semantic color variables, bound everywhere, with distinct meanings.

rules.text: Buy / Sell are actions (blue / coral); Gain / Loss are data (green / crimson). Keep the two pairs distinct so an action never reads as a result.
Danger buttons and icon buttons use status/critical, never finance/sell, so Sell never looks destructive.
text/inverse is the foreground on every solid fill; dark-mode fills are light enough to take dark text.
Use Color variables, never raw hex. Switch a frame's Color mode (Light / Dark) instead of recoloring.

doDont.title: Destructive actions use critical, not Sell
doDont.do: Danger uses status/critical, so it can't be mistaken for a Sell action.
doDont.dont: Sell coral on a delete button: traders learn coral means Sell, so this reads as a trade.

sections.name: Icons
sections.summary: A small set of outline glyphs that take their size and color from where they're used.

rules.text: 16px by default. Parent components bind icon width and height to Density → icon/size (12 / 16 / 16) or a size/* step; do the same when you place an icon yourself.

Icons have no color of their own: the component using one recolors its Glyph layer with a Color variable. When you place an icon yourself, bind its color to a Color variable (text/secondary for decoration, a status/*-strong color for meaning) so it follows Light/Dark.
An icon is never the only signal. Pair it with a label, or give an icon-only control an accessible name (Controls/Icon button's Label).
Supporting a label, or as an instance-swap value in Button, Status badge, and similar components.
It's the only way to convey meaning — pair it with text or an accessible name.

Sterling's Icon/* set is small. If an icon library is enabled in the file (e.g. Material Symbols), use its icons too: size them to 16 (or bind to icon/size) and bind their color to a Color variable so they follow Light/Dark. Button's Icon property can swap to any icon via the instance swap menu.

patterns.name: Filters, grid, and bulk actions
patterns.summary: The core data screen: narrow a large set of records, compare them in a grid, and act on a selection.
patterns.useWhen: People find, compare, and act on many records of the same kind (orders, positions, inventory).
patterns.dontUseWhen: There are only a handful of records (use a list or cards), or one record is being edited (use a form).

steps.label: Filters panel
steps.note: Filters sit on the left (2 of 12 columns). Inputs and selects narrow the rows; Apply runs the query and Reset clears it. Placeholders give examples, never labels.

steps.label: View and applied filters
steps.note: The View dropdown picks a named filter set (plus columns and sort); Save view saves the current one. Every applied filter is a chip, in sync with the panel: removing a chip clears its field, Clear all removes them all. No tabs here — tabs are for separate datasets (scopes), not for status views.

steps.label: Bulk action bar (only while rows are selected)
steps.note: The bulk action bar appears only while rows are selected, directly above the grid, and pushes the grid down — it never covers rows. Danger actions use status/critical.

steps.label: Grid
steps.note: In the grid, numeric columns are right-aligned with tabular figures; selected rows are tinted and checked; problem cells are flagged with a border and an icon.

steps.label: Pagination
steps.note: Pagination sits under the grid; Previous is disabled on the first page.

patterns.name: Bulk action bar
patterns.summary: What the bar above a grid says and offers as the selection changes. It appears only while rows are selected, directly above the grid, and pushes the grid down.
patterns.useWhen: People act on several rows at once (approve, export, delete).
patterns.dontUseWhen: An action applies to one row (put it in the row), or nothing can be selected (a read-only view has no bar).

steps.label: Some rows selected
steps.note: The count says how many rows are selected, in words. The bar has no checkbox: selecting every row on the page is the checkbox in the grid's header, and Clear selection is a button. Select all N matching extends the selection to every row that matches the filters, not only the page shown.

steps.label: All matching rows selected
steps.note: Once everything matching is selected, the count says so and the Select all link is hidden. Before a destructive action on this selection, ask for confirmation: it reaches rows the person can't see (see Confirmation dialog).

steps.label: An action that can't apply to this selection
steps.note: When an action can't apply to the selection, keep it in place, disabled, and say why in the hint beside it (Show hint). In code, link the hint to the button with aria-describedby.

steps.label: Read-only view
steps.note: A read-only view has no checkboxes and no bar. Danger actions use status/critical; reversible ones use a secondary button.

patterns.name: Filter panel and chips
patterns.summary: A panel sets the filters; chips above the grid show what's applied. The two always agree.
patterns.useWhen: A grid has several filterable columns and people combine filters.
patterns.dontUseWhen: There's one simple filter (put a select or a search field in the toolbar), or the condition defines the dataset itself (that's a criterion, not a filter).

steps.label: Filter panel
steps.note: The panel has one field per commonly filtered column; Add filter offers the rest. Apply runs the query and Reset clears every field. Placeholders give an example of the expected value, never the label.

steps.label: Applied filters as chips
steps.note: Every applied filter shows as a chip in plain words (Status is Open). Removing a chip clears its field in the panel, and choosing a view fills both. Changing the filters marks the view as edited (see Saved views).

patterns.name: Saved views
patterns.summary: A view is a named filter set, plus its columns and sort. People pick one from the View menu and can save their own.
patterns.useWhen: People come back to the same few filter sets (my items, flagged, large amounts).
patterns.dontUseWhen: The filters are one-off (chips are enough), or the choice switches to a different dataset (use tabs).

steps.label: View menu, open
steps.note: The menu groups predefined views and the person's own. Each option shows its filter set in muted text, so people know what they'll get before choosing. A view can also add columns.

steps.label: An edited view: Save view is enabled
steps.note: Changing a view's filters keeps its name and adds "· edited". Save view becomes available and saves the current filter set under Saved by me.

steps.label: An unchanged view: Save view is disabled
steps.note: While a view is unchanged, Save view stays visible but disabled, so its place doesn't shift.

patterns.name: Status chips
patterns.summary: A status chip says what state a record is in, with a tone, an icon, and one or two words.
patterns.useWhen: A record has a small set of states that people scan for (active, pending, flagged, blocked, draft).
patterns.dontUseWhen: The value is a number or free text, or the chip would show an applied filter (use a filter chip).

steps.label: One tone per meaning
steps.note: Positive: done or healthy. Info: in progress. Warning: needs attention. Critical: blocked or failed. Neutral: inactive or draft. Each tone has its own icon, so the status never depends on color alone.

steps.label: In a grid
steps.note: In a grid, status gets its own column, sized to the longest label. Use the same word for the same state everywhere.

steps.label: Long labels truncate
steps.note: Keep labels to one or two words. Longer labels truncate at 160px, so put detail in a neighboring column, not in the chip.

patterns.name: Warning and exception cells
patterns.summary: How a grid flags one value that needs attention or breaks a rule, without relying on color.
patterns.useWhen: One value in a row is outside a rule or limit, and people need to find it and see why.
patterns.dontUseWhen: The whole row has a state (use a status chip), or the grid couldn't load (use the error state).

steps.label: Normal, warning, error
steps.note: Warning marks a value that's allowed but needs attention; error marks one that blocks the action. Both add a border and an icon, and use darker ink on the tinted background.

steps.label: With keyboard focus
steps.note: The focus ring sits inside the flag's border, so a focused cell still shows that it's flagged.

steps.label: Say why, next to the value
steps.note: Say why in the row: a reason in a neighboring column, with the full rule in a tooltip. In code, include the reason in the cell's accessible name. Size the column with the icon allowance (numericColumnWidth with icon), so flagged values fit.

patterns.name: Confirmation dialog
patterns.summary: A dialog that asks before an action that can't be undone, or that reaches further than the person can see.
patterns.useWhen: The action is irreversible (delete), or it applies to rows beyond the visible page (all 120 matching).
patterns.dontUseWhen: The action is small and reversible: do it and offer Undo. Confirming everything teaches people to click through.

steps.label: An action that can't be undone
steps.note: The title asks the question, with the count. The primary button repeats the verb and the count, never "OK". Destructive actions use the danger button. Cancel is always there, and Escape closes the dialog.

steps.label: A selection that goes beyond the page
steps.note: A reversible action needs confirmation only when the selection goes beyond what's visible. The body says what's included and how to undo it.

steps.label: Over the screen, which is dimmed
steps.note: The dialog is modal: it sits in the middle of the screen it was opened from, and surface/scrim dims everything behind it, which can't be used until the dialog closes.

patterns.name: Form layout
patterns.summary: Create or edit one record: a single column of labeled fields, validation under each field, and one primary action.
patterns.useWhen: Creating or editing a single record with a few fields (a ticket, a setting, an order note).
patterns.dontUseWhen: Editing many records at once (use the grid and bulk actions), or a long process (split it into steps).

steps.label: Labels above, full width
steps.note: One column, labels above the fields, fields full width: the eye moves straight down, and labels stay visible while typing.

steps.label: Placeholder is an example
steps.note: Placeholder text is an example of the expected value, never the label — it disappears as soon as someone types.

steps.label: Error under the field (error-focus while fixing)
steps.note: Errors appear under the field with an icon and specific, fixable text. While the field is focused it keeps the red border and adds the focus ring (State = error-focus).

steps.label: Warning doesn't block saving
steps.note: Warnings (amber, with an icon) flag something to check but don't block saving; errors do.

steps.label: Checkbox with its label
steps.note: Outside a grid, checkboxes show their label (Show label on), so the whole label is the click target.

steps.label: Actions
steps.note: Actions sit at the bottom right: one primary action, with the secondary to its left.

patterns.name: Loading, empty, and error states
patterns.summary: What a data view shows before, instead of, or when it fails to show rows. Keep the header and filters so context isn't lost.
patterns.useWhen: Any data view that loads asynchronously or can come back empty.
patterns.dontUseWhen: Only some rows have problems (flag those cells instead), or filtering is local and instant (under ~300 ms, show nothing).

steps.label: Loading
steps.note: Loading: after ~300 ms, show skeleton rows under the real header, so the layout doesn't jump when rows arrive. Turn on the first row's label ("Loading rows…") and mark the grid aria-busy in code. Summary metrics use State = loading.

steps.label: Empty (no results)
steps.note: Empty: say why there are no rows and offer the way out — Clear filters for no results; for nothing yet, say what will appear and how to add it.

steps.label: Error
steps.note: Error: say what failed and offer Retry. The critical tone shows in the icon and title, not just color. Keep the header and filters so nothing is lost.
